utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar -- good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present, and I think Defence teams are -- we have a full house. The prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey. Today, as scheduled, we will start with the Rule 98 bis submissions, starting with Defence, of course. You are aware of our scheduling order, that we gave you a time limit, and you are requested not to exceed that time limit. Who is going first? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're going to split our argument. I'll take the first part, and Mr. Ostojic will take the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. Madam Registrar, if you could start timing now, please. Thank you. And before you start, Mr. Meek. Mr. McCloskey, is there any part of the indictment that you concede hasn't been proven at all or that you would like to withdraw? I'm asking you this question so that in that eventuality it would facilitate the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't intend to drop any counts, but I do believe, and I think we've discussed this before, there were -- one of the paragraphs relating to nine bodies in Potocari, there was no evidence on, and that's the main one that I recall right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Mr. Meek. You have started at 9.00 and eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution, all the Defence teams, all of the accused. I welcome you here. I want to say firstly that it has been a great honour and a privilege for me to represent Ljubisa Beara. This may well be the last time that I'm able to address this Chamber, and I hope that whatever I might be able to say today might help Your Honours in your deliberations on this case as we have seen it so far. Now, Your Honours, I would just like to talk a little bit about what has transpired in this courtroom the past 20 months and why there is no case, we feel, for Ljubisa Beara to answer. Your Honours, W.K. Clifford said "It is wrong always, everywhere and for everyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence." While the evidence adduced thus far in this trial must be viewed in a light most favourable to the OTP, is respectfully submitted that no reasonable, neutral and detached finder of fact, after deliberating and analysing the evidence, can, with a clear conscience, find that there is evidence that my client, Ljubisa Beara, also known as "the empty vessel," has been filled. In other words, why is there no evidence capable of supporting a conviction? We know, from the record and from months and months and years ago, that Ljubisa Beara was an empty vessel. We found this out after both sides had rested in the Blagojevic case in 2004, and Mr. McCloskey, a senior trial attorney, who by the way as we all know had been intimately involved in the Srebrenica cases, Krstic and Blagojevic, stated to that Court, on 29 September 2004, in his closing argument, page 12377 and 378, he said: "Beara is an empty vessel. Until Mladic gives him those orders, he doesn't have the right to command troops, he doesn't have any troops." 29 months later, we're here today in the instant trial, and on February 28th of 2007, at page 7927 of this transcript, line 24 and 25, the very same Prosecutor, Peter McCloskey, admitted once again in open court, in front of Your Honours, that Beara is an empty vessel, which is true, until he is filled with the orders of his commander, General Mladic. Your Honours, we believe that explicitly and implicitly, there is a promise by the Prosecution that they would bring forth evidence that would show that this empty vessel, Ljubisa Beara, would be filled, by evidence from the Prosecution side of direct orders from General Ratko Mladic. Your Honours, these are the words of the Prosecutor, and we believe they are a party admission that the OTP case against Ljubisa Beara is based on these purported mysterious orders, but we would like to know and we question where, when, how, and by which witnesses or exhibits was this allegation and promise fulfilled. Where, we ask, in the entire record is there any such evidence? We respectfully submit, Your Honours, that the record in this case thus far is devoid of any such orders from General Ratko Mladic to Ljubisa Beara, either directly, circumstantially, or otherwise. Ljubisa Beara stands charged before this Tribunal with eight counts, pursuant to the consolidated amended indictment. My lead counsel, Mr. Ostojic, will address in a moment the counts as they are set out in the indictment. Your Honours, the mere fact that we may not argue every count does not mean in any way, shape, or form that we believe the Office of the Prosecutor is correct or has met its burden under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As professional judges, you are, we know, aware of this position. The first thing that is very clear from all the evidence adduced by the Prosecution thus far is that the record is devoid of any evidence that Ljubisa Beara was anywhere in or around Srebrenica from the 1st of July to the 12th of July, 1995, except -- except for the testimony of Witness Zlatan Celanovic. His testimony, Your Honours, was uncorroborated by any other evidence including the evidence of the OTP analyst, Richard Butler, who on the 23rd of January, 2008, in this courtroom, at page 20230 of the record, line 17 through 24, stated basically that as far as he knew, there was no evidence of Mr. Beara's presence during those dates, in those times, at that place. Further, Your Honours, this witness, Celanovic, could not even be sure on which dates these purported sightings of Ljubisa Beara took place. And even assuming, for the sake of argument, that Witness Celanovic was not one of the bold-faced liars that Mr. McCloskey promised us, I submit and we submit, Your Honours, that the mere presence of Ljubisa Beara at a certain location is not in any way evidence of wrongdoing, culpability, complicity, let alone guilt of any criminal conduct. Furthermore, Your Honours, no evidence whatsoever has been brought before this Trial Chamber that Ljubisa Beara was anywhere in or around Potocari on 11 July -- from 11 July to 13th July 1995. Your Honours, not one iota of evidence has been brought forth that Ljubisa Beara was in Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel during the critical meetings held between Mladic and Dutch-Bat and later between Mladic and other higher officers from the VRS, including General Krstic, General Zivanovic, Colonel Jankovic, MUP officers including Vasic, some civilian leaders such as Deronjic, the Dutch-Bat representatives and the Muslim representatives. Your Honours, as a result of these meetings, it was that the evacuation of civilians was agreed. The agreement was reached between the representatives of the parties at those meetings who were negotiating at the Fontana Hotel on the 11th and the 12th of July, 1995. Your Honours, I must confess that it took many hours to debate and brainstorming before we actually made the decision to address Your Honours today under Rule 98 bis. At the end of the day, we jointly decided that an argument should be made pursuant to Rule 98 bis. However, having reviewed the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, it became brutally apparent that our chance of gaining much advantage by arguing this 98 bis motion was realistically merely a chance for the Office of the Prosecutor to understand the theory of our Defence and to understand the shortfalls in their case in chief. We submit most respectfully, Your Honours, that all of this, taken together, will help the OTP or could help the OTP in the preparation of their rebuttal case, even though, I submit, they could have called or brought forth the very same witnesses in their case in chief. However, having made the decision to give an argument, we are here. I have, throughout this Prosecution case, wondered a few things, not only directly related to my client, but to all of the accused. We wonder why the OTP and the Chief Prosecutor, who has been involved fully in the first two Srebrenica cases, all involving the same facts, can, in good faith, change the Prosecution theory to suit its needs. Further, Your Honours, we wonder why the OTP is allowed to do so. And, more importantly, we wonder how the Trial Chamber can determine which theory the OTP honestly believes is true. In the first two trials, the theory of the Defence was, as I understand, that security did it, there was a separate chain of command and security was the culprit behind this. However, as I understand it, Your Honour, the Prosecution that those cases took the opposite stance, insofar as their theory was very simply that these defences in the Krstic and Blagojevic cases were wrong. The Trial Chamber and the Appellate Chambers agreed in those cases. Further, Your Honours, we seriously wonder why such a learned prosecutor as my learned friend Mr. McCloskey has, from the beginning of this trial and even prior to that, at the 65 ter conference on 13 July 2006, at page 316, line 5 to 7, stated on the record his offence to an innocuous comment by co-counsel Julie Condon, quote, Mr. McCloskey said: "I would prefer her to come by me before she makes statements and statements that are going to go to my integrity." We wonder, Your Honour, just how it is that the Prosecutor, while pointing out his integrity and rejecting any notion of questioning of his ethics, truthfulness, veracity, honesty and legal character, can now argue that my client, Ljubisa Beara, also known as "the empty vessel," is some major player in the same events, trithing Krstic and Blagojevic. Your Honours, in relation to this issue, we've done much heavy thinking and we are hopeful and are sure that the Trial Chamber has likewise done so. In our respectful opinion, Your Honour, the notion that the Prosecution can shift theories from one case to the other, when the exact facts underlying them are the same, is not proper and is alien to us. Your Honours, we believe that dog won't hunt. Throughout this trial, we have wondered why the Office of the Prosecutor never used their in-house handwriting expert to examine those pages of the Zvornik officers' logbook, Exhibit 377, which had such notations as: "Colonel Beara, pass on the message," page 127 of that exhibit, English, and: "Colonel Beara is coming," page 129, English version. "Beara to call 155," page 156, English version. And once again: "Beara is coming," page 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We wonder, Your Honours, why it is that no one in the Office of the Prosecutor, with their massive staff, analysts, investigators, why they didn't bother to have the handwriting analysed or even thought about having it analysed. Your Honours, we wonder why the OTP never once showed witnesses or suspect/witnesses proper photo lineups, except one, or live lineups when it came to our client, Mr. Beara. We believe that the one incident where a photo was shown to a witness, which Mr. Ostojic will go into in greater detail, was totally worthless, from a legal standpoint. Your Honour, we wonder why the OTP witnesses who claim to have sighted Ljubisa Beara all gave the same general vague description, a description, Your Honours, which would fit numerous VRS officers at that time. A mere review of the film of General Zivanovic's retirement party will confirm this fact. Your Honours, we wonder why, during certain witness interviews, the interviewee had his status changed from witness to that of suspect in the middle of the interview, and then after the witness had given incriminatory information concerning Ljubisa Beara, his status was changed back to that of a witness. Your Honours, we further wonder why there were off-the-record, unrecorded conversations with these suspect/witnesses who suddenly changed their story and, we believe, changed their story to fit the Prosecution's new theory in this case. Your Honours, all of these interviews that I've just talked about, we believe and have unsuccessfully argued, were in violation of Rule 43 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Your Honours, if Ljubisa Beara is who they say he is, a planner, close to or part of Mladic's inner circle, why is Ljubisa Beara not seen in any video, any clips, any photos, with Mladic, Krstic, Zivanovic, Vasic and others? Why is that, we wonder. Your Honours, if Ljubisa Beara is who they say he is, why was Ljubisa Beara not at General Zivanovic's retirement party, along with Mladic and other high-ranking VRS officers? Your Honours, we wonder why OTP investigators threw away and/or destroyed their field notes, especially, Your Honour, field notes of an unrecorded four-day interview with PW-168, the Prosecution's star witness, at a time that he was still a suspect, and this investigator, the record reflects, kept those notes for approximately two years before he departed this Tribunal, and didn't think they were needed, so he just destroyed them. The OTP, Your Honour, are going to tell you, when it comes their time to speak, that PW-168 is a credible witness. We submit, respectfully, that PW-168 is as crooked as a dog's hind leg. Make no mistake about it. Please don't be fooled, like the Prosecution was fooled, by his slick lies and deceptions. We ask that you think about that. Your Honours, I fortunately or unfortunately have grown up surrounded by lawyers, judges, and politicians. A bad combination, without any doubt. My father was a lawyer and then a trial judge. My grandfather, two aunts and an uncle were also lawyers, plus an uncle by marriage who is a lawyer and a politician. I thus learned about the law at a very early age, and in that process I was always taught that there is a right and there is a wrong, that it's wrong to presume a person charged with a crime is guilty, that it's wrong to not allow an accused person the right to a fair and public trial and to effective assistance of counsel. Frankly, Your Honours, my father taught me not to believe anything I heard or read and only half of what I saw. Your Honours, you know, I was also taught that bad facts make bad law. This truth I really didn't fully understand until I started practicing law and trying cases in 1979. And, Your Honours, no one who has followed this trial, the Blagojevic trial or the Krstic trial, or has even read the indictment in this case, can dispute that there are bad facts in this case. I have been reminded during this trial on several occasions that hope springs eternal, and being the optimist that I am, I pray that what flows from the bad facts of this case is not bad law. Your Honours, I must confess that I am, truthfully and very respectfully, disillusioned by the conduct of these trials in this Tribunal. I believe that history will judge all of us in these proceedings, and I believe that ultimately it will not be whether the accused were found guilty or not guilty, nor the sentences given to those convicted, but whether those accused, those human beings, like each of us, received a fair trial before they were convicted and sentenced to live behind bars in a steel cage for years and years. Your Honours, liberty is a lucre that the OTP has to barter with for their witness testimony. Liberty, the most precious commodity of all. I ask: Who would not trade a year's salary for their liberty for that same period of time? I bring this up only for your consideration when you are analysing the testimony of Prosecution witnesses to determine if it is capable of supporting a conviction. We submit it is not. Your Honours, my learned friend Peter McCloskey told you, on the 24th of August, 2006, in this very courtroom, that in the course of testimony, some ten years after these events, there's more people willing to talk, more people who will directly implicate one or more of the accused, and he also said that at the end of the OTP witness list, there are a long list of VRS and MUP people. But a word of caution here, he said, "Many of these witnesses will not be telling you the full truth. Many will be going back and forth." He said, however, he was confident that you would be able to glean the truth from these witnesses, and he told you: "... and in fact, even in the lies, you can find the truth." We submit, Your Honours, that even a half truth is a lie. Further, Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. McCloskey told you, "I think there is something to be had from this witness, even though he is a bold-faced liar, and I think we glean something from his bold-faced lie." Your Honours, we glean something different from these bold-faced liars that Mr. McCloskey was speaking about in his opening statement. We glean that these liars are not credible witnesses, and it would be a travesty of international justice to base any part of a guilty verdict on their lying testimony. Your Honours, these witnesses that the Office of the Prosecutor brought forth, many, many of them came here not to testify, but they came here to test a lie. And we respectfully submit that they surely did. We ask Your Honours that when analysing the testimony of the OTP witnesses, keep in mind that the OTP put forth witnesses it knew would lie. This practice, once again, is alien to my lead counsel and myself, and we believe that in most jurisdictions, if not all, it is barred and forbidden. Your Honours, the OTP put forth witnesses that had made deals with them for a lesser sentence, for their liberty, and keep in mind that common sense tells you that if you're eating a bowl of beef stew and you bite into a rotten piece of beef, a rotten piece of meat, you don't throw out that one rotten piece of meat and keep on eating the stew, do you? Common sense tells you you throw out the whole bowl. However, the Office of the Prosecutor would have you throw out the rotten meat, the rotten lies in their witness testimony, and keep on listening, hoping to find some truth. We believe, Your Honours, this is illogical, unfounded, and ludicrous. In analysing the evidence given by the OTP witnesses, even in a light most favourable to the Prosecution, bear in mind that many of them the Prosecution did not tell us exactly which ones lied or were going to. We respectfully submit that more than a few fit the category described by my learned colleague Mr. McCloskey in his opening statement. For example, Your Honours, for inter alia PW-168, PW-102, Witness Celanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Silanovic"], PW-161, PW-162, Bircakovic, Babic, Peric, these are a few examples. Your Honour, these witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For the sake of the record, can I get the correct spelling of "Celanovic"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's definitely spelled out wrongly here in the transcript, but it's "C" for "Charlie," "E" for "Echo" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: B-I-R-C-A-K-O-V-I-C, I believe Your Honour. These are just a few examples. And, Your Honours, in our humble opinion and analysis, these witnesses were nothing more or nothing less than walking, talking pieces of deception. We merely ask Your Honours, in your deliberation and analysis, to take these submissions into account, and the testimony, when you look at it, evaluate it, analyse it, don't forget there's a motive to lie and point the finger at others in many instances. Your Honours, courts over time have always looked at an accomplice's testimony with caution. In a 1680 case from England, one hailing pleas of the Crown, the judge stated: "The Defendant admonishes us to heed the lessons of history by skewing the corrupt bargain that produces accomplice testimony. He invokes vintage authority with the observation, 'Truly it is hard to take away the life of any person upon such a witness that swears to saves his own.'" That was 1680, Your Honour. Your Honours, we submit that criminals are likely to say and do almost anything to get what they want, especially if what they want is to get out of trouble. This willingness to do anything includes not only truthfully spilling the beans on friends and relatives, but also lying, committing perjury, manufacturing evidence, soliciting others to corroborate their lies with more lies. How many times have we seen that in this case. Double-crossing anyone with who they come in contact with, including and especially the Prosecutor. Your Honour, one of the basic tenets of the jurisprudence of any civilised nation is that a trial is a search for the truth, and by that it is not meant the purchased truth, the bartered-for truth, but the unvarnished truth. It may well be that we must live sometimes with bargained-for pleas of guilty, but we don't have to give a receipt stamp "paid in full for your damning testimony," or, "You will be paid according to how well you can convince, even though it may be in the face of lies." Your Honours, we submit trustworthiness is a keystone and hallmark of any judicial system that seeks recognition for its role in a civilised society, and we believe, Your Honours, that it is time for this International Tribunal to announce boldly and firmly that the judicial search for the truth here cannot be reconciled with the virtual purchase of perjury. It is respectfully submitted, Your Honours, that there is something to be had from these lying witnesses only if the Trial Chamber totally ignores the simple truth, that in life you can bargain for and buy almost anything. You can bargain for and buy mansions, villas, priceless works of art, you can bargain for and buy all the creature comforts you can conjure up in your mind, but thank God there is some things you can't buy or some things you can't bargain for. You can't buy or bargain for wisdom. You can't buy or bargain for justice, because if you do, what you get is injustice. You can't buy or bargain for love, because if you do, it isn't love that you get, and you can't buy or bargain for truth, because it isn't truth that you get. It's testimony, with a cloud of suspicion hanging over it. You can't buy and you can't bargain for testimony, and that is, we submit, what the OTP has done in this case, especially with their star witness, PW-168, and that's why their case, we believe, is in the state it is at the present time. Your Honours, hanging on the one of the walls in the oldest courthouse in England are the words: "In this hallowed place of justice, the Crown never loses, because when liberty of an Englishman is preserved against false witnesses, the Crown wins." Your Honour, I learned many years ago that the prosecution never loses. My father explained to me because if they get a conviction, they've won. If they get an acquittal, they've won also because justice is done. So the prosecutor never win, and they can win both ways. On 21 of August, 2006, Carla Del Ponte said in her opening statement page 381, line 235: "The surviving victims of Srebrenica crimes yearn for justice, not vengeance." We say to you that we agree with this sentiment, that the surviving victims yearn for justice, not vengeance, and we also submit that to convict the guilty is not necessarily the end of the game, is not what the OTP should be looking for. What the victims, we believe, do not want to see is an innocent man convicted, as this would, Your Honours, do a disservice and an injustice to the victims. Again, Your Honours, to convict an innocent man would do disservice to the victims of Srebrenica and is not, Your Honours, in any manner, as Ms. Del Ponte told us, an important step towards a cause and a cause for hope. We believe that only contributes to the pain and suffering of the surviving victims. Your Honour, a review of the wrongful conviction cases throughout the world indicate that those who are wrongfully convicted were victims of these problems: Inaccurate eyewitness identifications, unreliable jailhouse informants or snitches, failure of police and prosecutors to disclose exculpatory evidence and faulty forensics. We've seen some of the faulty forensics through our cross-examinations in the OTP's case, and we believe that in the Defence cases, should there be any, that we will prove not only faulty mathematics but faulty DNA submissions also. Centred on wrongful convictions, the Northwestern University school of Law in Chicago, Illinois, identified four types of false and or unreliable evidence, false testimony by informant or snitch witnesses, two, incorrect eyewitness identification, three, false confessions which tend to point the finger at others, four, false or unreliable forensic evidence or junk science. In closing, Your Honours, I would like to say that it has been an honour to be in front of this Trial Chamber and a privilege, and it's been a greater privilege to represent Ljubisa Beara as a client. I would just like to share with you something that Justice Jackson, who was a Justice of the United States Supreme Court, one of the architects of Nuremberg, and you may have heard it but I'll say it again. He said: "If good-faith trials are sought, that is another matter. All experience teaches that there are certain things you cannot do under the guise of judicial trial. Courts try cases, but cases also try courts. You must put no man on trial before anything that is called a court under the forms of judicial proceedings if you're not willing to see him freed if not proven guilty." I want to lastly thank everyone here, the staff, the Registry, the UN security people, the technical people, especially the interpreters for putting up with my accent and my cadence, and likewise, Your Honours, for putting up with me, and your struggle and your patience, Your Honours. I also want to thank my lead counsel, John Ostojic, for his guidance, his leadership, his direction and his counselling. The two of us have spent quite a bit of time, two years, brainstorming, bouncing things off of each other's heads, and I've got to admit, Your Honours, it's been a long, strange, and interesting trip. I would like to just, in further closing, quote from a great American, Martin Luther King. Martin Luther King said: "In justice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny. Whatever affects one directly affects all directly." He wrote that in a letter from the Birmingham jail on the 16th of April, 1963. I thank you Your Honours very much. It's been my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it you are leaving us, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I read your intervention meaning that you will be leaving us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Anything is possible, Your Honour, and we can certainly address that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic. You are starting at 9.51.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Mr. President, honourable Judges, fellow colleagues and Mr. Beara, we respectfully submit that despite the rigid and inflexible rules of Rule 98 bis, that indeed, based on the evidence that is presented, that this honourable Trial Chamber should acquit on specifically counts 7 and 8 of the second amended consolidated indictment. Permit me to share with you why. By way of background, we have seen the allegations, we have heard the promises, and we have seen and heard the evidence, and we now know and respectfully submit that the promises were unfulfilled and the allegations indeed unsubstantiated. The allegation that Mr. Beara planned, organised, assisted, supervised, or facilitated, or otherwise aided and abetted in the transportation of civilians in either Srebrenica or Zepa, was not proven. Ljubisa Beara is not criminally responsible, and therefore an acquittal is warranted. I hope to walk through with you some of this evidence. First I would like to address Zepa and the allegations both in count 7 of forcible transfer as well as count 8, deportation. We've heard, in essence, from I believe ten witnesses in connection with the movement of people involved in Zepa. The key questions, I believe, that we have to ask ourselves in determining whether Mr. Beara was involved is: First, when did the transportation begin? Paragraph 71 of the indictment suggests that the movement and transportation of people from Zepa commenced on July 25th, 1995. OTP analyst Mr. Butler claims that it was the 26th, and admittedly he said he was going off memory. The next critical question, we submit, that must be asked in connection with Zepa is: How long did the movement of these civilians last? It lasted, as Mr. Butler suggested, one, two days maximum, which would end approximately on the 28th or 29th of July. When you review the evidence on whole, you'll find that there was no evidence of Ljubisa Beara's involvement, either from documents, orders, intercepts, logbooks, or personal diaries, suggesting that he was near or around the area of Zepa when there was a commencement of the movement of the civilian population. The only evidence that even Mr. Butler could find that may remotely suggest any involvement by Mr. Beara with respect to Zepa in general were three intercepts that purport to have been captured with his voice, two on the 1st of August and one on the 2nd of August, 1995. We'll deal with that specifically in a moment, but when we deal with planning of the movement of people, Mr. Butler, on the 23rd of January, 2008, specifically on page 20217, lines 13 through 20, stated: "I have no evidence that he, Mr. Beara, was part of it." With respect to organisation, assistance, supervision, or facilitation of the movement of those civilians from Zepa, again we turn to Mr. Butler, and on the same page, 20217, lines 21 through 24, on the 23rd of January, 2008, he says: "I give you the same answer. I have no information. Therefore, you know, on a lack of information, I agree with you." Butler agrees, indeed, that there was no evidence whatsoever that Ljubisa Beara was involved in the forcible transfer or deportation of the civilian population in Zepa. In fact, and I believe it is undisputed, that there is not a shred of evidence inferring or establishing Ljubisa Beara's purported involvement in Zepa. Butler continues, when he tells us on page 20213, lines 9 through 10: "I don't believe we have any intercepts or any other information pertaining to Ljubisa Beara, his whereabouts during that period, namely, July 16th through the 31st, 1995." We didn't need to ask Mr. Butler what he meant when he said "any other information," but we can logically and predictably understand that that meant no intercepts, no documents, no orders, no logbooks, no personal diaries, no Bosnian Muslim witnesses, not even the liars that the OTP from time to time paraded in this courtroom, no evidence we suggest mandates an acquittal. OTP, throughout witnesses -- through their witnesses, they indeed concede that there was no evidence Ljubisa Beara on these two counts. If forcible transfer and deportation -- and/or deportation of Zepa population began on July 25th or 26th and ended on the 28th or 29th, it is rather plain that the OTP, through its witnesses and in summary fashion, concede that there is no evidence against Mr. Beara relating to either of these two counts with respect to Zepa, and therefore, under the prevailing law, as rigid and inflexible as it may be, no reasonable trier of fact could ever find, respectfully, against Ljubisa Beara on these two counts, and therefore must dismiss the same. The Court asked Mr. President a question during some of our cross-examinations, and you wondered about joint criminal enterprise. Since there is no evidence, documents, intercepts or witnesses which remotely link Ljubisa Beara to any involvement in the movement of civilians from Zepa at any time from start to finish, this discussion, we submit, is not relevant, unnecessary and unwarranted. But what about the intercepts? The three intercepts, as I've identified, were from the 1st of August and the 2nd of August, 1995. With respect to these two intercepts -- with these three intercepts, they clearly were captured well after the forcible transfer and/or deportation was planned and organised and facilitated and completed. You cannot and should not, respectfully, consider them in relation to counts 7 and 8 of the second amended consolidated indictment. However, not knowing what the Trial Chamber will do, if we assume that the Trial Chamber accepts these intercepts in some fashion as some sort of link with the movement or transportation of civilians, we believe that a close review of these intercepts do not reflect or reveal criminal conduct, and in fact support that Mr. Beara, if he was the one that was in these intercepts, indeed conducted himself in a very legal and professional manner in discussing prisoners of war and trying to make sure that they were being registered with the International Red Cross and other organisations. In a nutshell with respect to Zepa, there's only three intercepts that may even be considered. I suggest that they shouldn't, and even if they are considered, they are indeed exculpatory and do not prove that Ljubisa Beara in any instance was involved in the movement or transfer of the civilian population in Zepa, and therefore we once again request that with respect to counts 7, forcible transfer, and count 8, deportation, as it relates to Zepa, that they be dismissed. Your Honours, in the interests of time, I'm going to move to the movement of people from Srebrenica. That allegation is set out in count 7 of the second amended consolidated indictment, forcible transfer. The key paragraphs, we suggest, that you should review, among others, is specifically paragraphs 61 through 64. I think the same questions that we asked about Zepa are pertinent for Srebrenica. When did the transportation or movement of people commence? The movement of the civilian population from Srebrenica commenced on the 12th of July and ended on the 13th of July, 1995. In fact, that is undisputed, and we can refer to the adjudicated facts, specifically fact 203 and 219. The threshold question that we've asked from time to time, through witnesses, is whether it was forcible transfer or an evacuation. We contend that it was an evacuation, given the presence, assistance, and participation of Dutch-Bat, among others, and not forcible transfer. We do not rely solely on the presence, assistance and participation of Dutch-Bat. We believe other factors may further assist this Trial Chamber in reaching the proper conclusion that it was not forcible transfer, but rather an evacuation. If we examine the testimony of Mr. Kingori, who was here recently with us from Kenya, and specifically look at Exhibit P00493, it clearly states that the inhabitants of Zepa -- I mean of Srebrenica, 80 to 85 per cent were refugees themselves, taking another factor that the Bosnian Muslim men, both military and non-military men, voluntarily abandoned the civilians and formed a long column, seeking to go through the dark forest one day before the evacuation even started. Analysis as to whether it was evacuation or forcible transfer. We suggest that the movement of the civilians from Srebrenica was an evacuation, not a forcible transfer, and we must place it in context with the full and complete picture as to what the civilians of Srebrenica desired or decided at that time. Given that 80 per cent or more of the population in Srebrenica, in July of 1995, were refugees or displaced persons, they never considered Srebrenica their home, but rather temporarily an intermittent residence. Given that the Bosnian Muslim military and non-military males, for whatever reason, abandoned the enclave voluntarily, and the civilians could not and would not have decided anything other than to leave and permit the evacuation with Dutch-Bat to commence. In a general sense, that's the movement of the civilian population in Srebrenica. To relate it specifically as it relates to Ljubisa Beara, despite what you may decide, and even if you decide that there was sufficient evidence to find forcible transfer at this stage of the proceedings, respectfully, we nonetheless suggest that you must acquit Ljubisa Beara on this count. Why? The evidence that was brought forth here, both the video evidence, the documentary evidence, the evidence from the witnesses themselves, we saw who the participants were, we saw where the participants met, and we know from witnesses what was said at those meetings prior to the actual evacuation or transfer or movement of the population from Srebrenica. Where was Mladic with regard to the events leading up to the movement of the people from Srebrenica? We saw Mladic in Bratunac, Hotel Fontana, on three occasions at least. We saw Mladic in Srebrenica. We saw Mladic in Potocari, and we saw Mladic in Sandici. Never, ever was Mladic near or even in the presence of Ljubisa Beara at any of those locations, places, or times. We submit that those are concrete facts that the Court must take into consideration when evaluating Mr. Beara's culpability with respect to this count involving the movement of the population in Srebrenica. Never, ever was there evidence of any kind to suggest, infer, or establish that Ljubisa Beara was near or present at the locations when purportedly decisions to evacuate or forcibly transfer the population was made. Butler exposed himself on this issue when we asked him specifically, "Did you have any evidence of Mr. Beara being at Bratunac in the Hotel Fontana?" It's a classic example, in my opinion, of how the OTP and its former staff member analyst make unsubstantiated leaps of faith, misguided interpretations and erroneous conclusions. When I asked Mr. Butler, on the 23rd of January, 2008, to confirm that in fact there was no evidence whatsoever that would place Mr. Beara at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac for any of those three meetings on the 11th or 12th of July, 1995, Mr. Butler could have been honest. Instead, he chose to make it up as he went along. First he said, at page 20232, line 6 through 14: "I believe there are some records that place him, Mr. Beara, at the Hotel Fontana, that he'd had a room there during the relevant period, but he's not listed as one of the participants in any of the meetings." Mr. Butler went so far afield and said not only that he believed Ljubisa Beara was at the Hotel Fontana, he suggested and stated explicitly that he had a room there. Upon further questioning, Mr. Butler seemingly realised his mistake, and for the second time, instead of just being honest, he chose to waffle and to keep things vague. He said, on pages 20232, lines 20 through 21: "I don't recall whether or not Colonel Beara was one of those listed officers. I mean, we have those records, but I just don't recall at the moment whether he was one of those officers who had a room or not there." Meaning at the Hotel Fontana. Indeed, as we know, based on my conversation with my learned friend after that testimony, and based on a review of the records and documents from the Hotel Fontana, Mr. Beara was not listed as a participant in that meeting, and Mr. Beara never had a room for that entire month at any time at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. Those, in our opinion, were the critical meetings, as the Prosecution suggests, where some planning and organising was done to conduct the transportation of the civilian population from Srebrenica. Ljubisa Beara unequivocally, I suggest, was not present at any of those meetings and was not present on or around the area when those decisions were being made or implemented. When we look at the allegations in the indictment, I have no doubt and I am confident that the OTP will concede that Ljubisa Beara is in no way involved in the forcible removal of the civilian population from Srebrenica. Ljubisa Beara is not even mentioned or referenced in paragraph 61, 62, or 64 of count 7, which involves forcible transfer in the second amended consolidated indictment. Those are the four paragraphs, and I've mentioned three. With respect to paragraph 63, there is a reference to Mr. Beara. Paragraph 63, in my submission, does not belong in count 7 of this document. It deals not with civilians; it deals with Bosnian Muslim military and non-military men from the column. The Bosnian Muslims from the column who left, they left on their own volition and were not, theoretically or practically, forcibly removed. If this Trial Chamber, respectfully, in my view, unreasonably finds that the Bosnian men from the column were indeed forcibly transferred out of Srebrenica, it nonetheless, in our view, must acquit Mr. Beara of the allegations in count 7 of the indictment. The questions remain: Did the OTP prove, through the witnesses such as Egbers, that Ljubisa Beara was in Bratunac, as alleged? Why did they not call Zoran Modric, who was also there, who they have interviewed, who they have taken statements from? Why did they not call other members of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment? Why didn't they call other Dutch-Bat witnesses who were with Mr. Egbers on the dates he claims he saw Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba? In addition to failing to provide or calling corroborating evidence on the purported presence of Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba, Egbers's testimony is nothing more than speculative, conjecture, and a misidentification. The description was erroneous, the time period too short for him to evaluate. Egbers himself never confirmed or hinted that Ljubisa Beara was involved in the purported forcible transfer of the captured Bosnian Muslim males at Nova Kasaba on July 14th, 1995. Needless to say, if we examine all the evidence put forth by the Prosecution on this issue, we must look to three other witnesses. One, Milorad Bircakovic; two, (redacted), and, again, three, again Egbers. If we draw up a timeline in respect of these three witnesses, you'll find that this Court cannot accept their testimony because it is in conflict. Each claim to have seen Mr. Beara and had a purported meeting with him on July 14th, 1995. Bircakovic claims that it was at approximately 8.30 in Zvornik. (redacted) claims that it was at approximately 9.00 or 9.30 in Bratunac. Egbers claims it was at 9.30 or 10.00 at Nova Kasaba. Impossible. This Court should and indeed must dismiss all three witnesses on the basis that they're not credible, that they are not believable. Despite what I believe are these blatant defects and obvious flaws, the Trial Chamber may at this stage somehow view the testimony as believable. It should respectfully, nonetheless, acquit Mr. Beara, because the removal of the Bosnian Muslim civilian population from Potocari and Srebrenica was completed on the evening of July 13th by 2000 hours, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be careful when you are mentioning names. This is not just you, Mr. Ostojic, but all the others, please, to make sure that you are not mentioning any protected witnesses by their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I've worked hard to try to avoid that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it should be easy, actually. You should have had a list of these ready at hand. Anyway, let's proceed. We are making the redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We believe that the testimony of these witnesses, be it Bircakovic, PW-162, and Egbers, were not corroborated with any other witnesses. All occurred the day after the completion of the movement of the civilian population from Srebrenica. All three of these individuals, we believe, it is impossible to suggest that they and only they saw Mr. Beara at that given time. There was absolutely no one else who saw Mr. Beara but these three individuals. Is it possible that he could travel from one point to the next point and then the third point in such a short time, and yet have meetings with these people from anywhere from 10 minutes to 30 minutes? I suggest that if we plainly look at a map, you'll find that it is indeed impossible. None of the paragraphs relevant to count 7, forcible transfer, 61, 62, 63 and 64, have been proven, and thus an acquittal is appropriate and warranted as it relates to Mr. Beara. This honourable Chamber is asked from time to time about joint criminal enterprise, and the Prosecution, as reflected in the indictment, has selected to declare themselves with the third form, extended joint criminal enterprise. We believe the evidence, when you weigh it, not at this time, but when you examine the evidence at this stage as it relates to Mr. Beara, what they've proven is perhaps collective guilt, but they've not proven any joint criminal enterprise or any participation of that joint criminal enterprise by Mr. Beara. We've tried to establish, through some of our questions, a timeline for Mr. Beara. He was not, as we've heard, noticed by anyone, including their analyst, who thoroughly seemed to have examined evidence to find some culpability of accused, he couldn't find any evidence from the 1st through the 12th of July, 1995. He couldn't find any evidence, as it relates to Mr. Beara, from the 17th through the 31st of July, 1995. When we discussed this third variant of extended joint criminal enterprise, we speak of knowledge, and if we look at the intercepts to determine what, if anything, Mr. Beara knew or should have known at that time, you'll find that there's only two options for us to really examine. If you accept or believe the OTP evaluation, analysis, and interpretation with respect to the intercept evidence relating to Mr. Beara, the two logical options are as follows: One, that Mr. Beara did not have any knowledge of the events that were going on at that time. If we take, for example, the intercept 65 ter 1177, a purported conversation with Zivanovic, or that Beara allegedly is calling for Zivanovic on the 15th of July, 1995, the question that Mr. McCloskey should have asked is: Why would Ljubisa Beara, if he knew what was going on at that time, why would he call General Zivanovic? Mr. Beara should have known, as everyone knew, that at that time there was a replacement for the Drina Corps Command from General Zivanovic to General Krstic. If this was Beara at the intercept, as they allege, Mr. Beara had no knowledge. If it wasn't Mr. Beara, then we shouldn't use the intercept at all to determine whether he was involved or had knowledge of any joint criminal enterprise or the involvement of criminal conduct based on that. We discussed and we found another issue relating to this extension 155. Now, Mr. Butler, in an attempt to be genuine with us, he coined it "a little anomaly." When asked how could Mr. Beara, if this indeed, as they allege, is an extension for the Main Staff, if this is Mr. Beara calling on this intercept, how could he not know the extension 155 was for the Main Staff? Butler calls it a little anomaly, but indeed all it is is prosecutorial parlance for saying there is reasonable doubt, and he couldn't say that to us. If Mr. Beara was not on that intercept, then you must not consider those intercepts against him relating to joint criminal enterprise and the third variant. One other example, although we have many that we'll share with the Court, was again 65 ter 1178. What no one wanted to discuss in that interview was that purportedly Mr. Beara was there with a gentleman by the name of Lukic. The Prosecution claims that it was a man by the name of Milan Lukic from Visegrad who was not a commander, not an assistant commander, but a mere soldier in a battalion or brigade. If we look closely at that intercept, you'll find that the person who captured the conversation and purports that it was Mr. Beara says that, "Lukic is here with his driver. I dare say that there are two things we have to discuss here: One, it's impossible that a soldier such as Milan Lukic, at the age of 23 years at that time, if not younger, had his own driver. He was neither a commander, assistant commander, in charge of not even a troop. The prosecution offers these suggestions, but fails to explain them thoroughly. In the brief moments that we have, I'd like to talk about Mr. Celanovic which I think was an open witness. Mr. Celanovic testified here and he claimed that he saw Mr. Beara in or around Bratunac. The testimony, we believe, is not reliable. And I understand under Rule 98, you have to determine whether you should believe it and consider it in the light most favourable to the Prosecution. There's no corroborating evidence as it relates to Mr. Celanovic, but if you really read his testimony, he suggested that he basically had an encounter with Mr. Beara, and they basically took a walk, and they took a walk from one building all the way across town to the next, unseen by anyone. No one came up to them, no assistants, no other colleagues, no other soldiers or members of the Bratunac Brigade. Mr. Celanovic was walking supposedly across town. He inspected, allegedly, the POWs, and they were planning, purportedly, where the POWs would go next. There is no corroboration that Mr. Beara was there at the time suggested by Mr. Celanovic. Was the town empty? And I'm sorry for using that word, because I know my friend is sensitive with it. Was the town vacant or desolate? Of course not. He's suggesting to us that there were buses there, that there were many soldiers there, many officers there, that we can draw from many different witnesses. No one, other than Celanovic, saw, purportedly, Mr. Beara there. Even if this Court accepts and believes Mr. Celanovic, despite the fact that his testimony was vague and, in my view, inconsistent and truly unbelievable, given the circumstances that he described it, we believe that that encounter does not involve any criminal culpability on the part of Mr. Beara. Here's why: If we recall his testimony, he said the conversation was short and to the point. The conversation, in all respects, was about the screening and the interrogation of POWs. There was no conversation about doing anything other than what's legally prescribed both under the former Yugoslav and the VRS laws as well as that which is indicated in the Geneva Conventions in dealing with POWs. So either way, if we accept Mr. Celanovic's testimony, although I don't because we believe Mr. Beara was not there at the time that he claims, it nonetheless doesn't provide any scintilla of evidence for any of the counts or allegations in my learned friend has asserted against Mr. Beara. We are focusing, indeed, on count 7 with this testimony, and we believe that even if you accept Celanovic, you must still acquit Ljubisa Beara on this count. There are two other brief issues that I'd like to discuss. There were very few identifications, proper identifications, performed by the Office of the Prosecutor. One we do have that they conducted, and that was with the witness who I understand was in open session, Drazen Erdemovic. With respect to Drazen Erdemovic, my learned friend and I were able to come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There was some confusion with other testimony and witnesses with this regard. With respect to Drazen Erdemovic, we're really focusing on the Branjevo Military Farm and Pilici. My learned friend and I made a stipulation in that regard, and we filed it on the 7th of May, 2007. If we closely look at that stipulation, the Court will find that it was significant Drazen Erdemovic did not identify or recall ever seeing Mr. Beara where others claim he may have been, but what's important to note is the energy that the Prosecution used in trying to confirm that Mr. Beara was there. They got word from Mr. Erdemovic that he saw the individual, a lieutenant colonel or colonel, from some BBC television show while he was in prison. They immediately sent their team over there, got a copy of that tape, got additional copies of that tape, showed it to him, and he did not confirm that that was Mr. Beara. Subsequently, for the first time, they showed him a picture of Mr. Beara, and it's attached as an exhibit or an annex to our filing of the 7th of May, 2007, and Mr. Erdemovic confirmed at that time that that individual in that picture, who is Mr. Beara, was not the individual he saw at any time at either Branjevo Military Farm or at Pilici. We've chosen --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to confirm and get our facts straight, which I think is important, Mr. Erdemovic never said it was a colonel. He's always said "Lieutenant Colonel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Court has heard the testimony of other Prosecution witnesses who have said that they don't know if it was a lieutenant colonel or colonel at any given sighting. Whether Erdemovic said it was a colonel or lieutenant colonel, I believe that the Prosecution sought to implicate Mr. Beara by showing he was present at that site, they would not have shown him the picture of Mr. Beara had they not at least believed or wanted to believe or wished to believe that it was Mr. Beara. They showed him the picture, and Mr. Erdemovic rejected them. They did not do that with any of the other witnesses that were brought before you who they claim had encounters with Mr. Beara. We've chosen, Your Honours and Mr. President, to selectively isolate with respect to counts 7 and 8. By no means do we suggest they've proven or met their burden of proof with respect to the other six counts. We do ask that Your Honours use your discretion and decide whether other counts can also be dismissed, which we believe they can. We strongly feel that if this Court outlines the timeline of both the evacuation and movement of people in Zepa, as well as the evacuation and movement of the civilian population in Srebrenica, you'll find that Ljubisa Beara not only was never near those areas, did not participate in any of the meetings to plan or organise any such either evacuation, forcible transfer, or deportation. I humbly thank Your Honours for listening to us and for giving us the opportunity address you, and we believe the evidence will speak for itself that these two counts should and indeed must be dismissed as it relates to Mr. Beara. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. We'll have a break now. I allowed us to go beyond the time. Who is going next? Okay. We'll have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. You're starting at 11.02.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning, colleagues. As usual, my colleagues representing the accused Beara are a tough act to follow, but that being said, I will endeavour to keep my submissions both interesting and as short as possible. Mr. President, the Prosecution closed its case on 6 February, and I have the honour today of addressing the Trial Chamber in accordance with the order issued on 29 November 2007. Going straight to the point, my aim today is to respectfully request that Drago Nikolic, the accused I represent in this case, along with Mrs. Nikolic, be acquitted at this stage for counts 7 and 8, as well as count 2, pursuant to Rule 98 bis. My submissions today will last no more than 90 minutes, as authorised by the Trial Chamber, hopefully shorter. Turning to the law applicable to Rule 98 bis submissions, a procedure unknown to most continental law systems, I do not intend to spend much time. That being said, the applicable standard for Rule 98 bis submissions is well established in the case law of the International Tribunal, and I refer the Trial Chamber to the latest decision in the case the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic in Rule 98 bis. In that case, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber held that the test to be applied is whether there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the particular accused on the count in question. The Trial Chamber went on to say: "Therefore, where there is no evidence to sustain a count, the motion will be granted." Furthermore, where there is some evidence but it is such that, taken at its highest, a Trial Chamber could not convict on it, the motion will also be granted. While I won't spend much time on the applicable law to Rule 98 bis, I do wish to stress, Mr. President, the importance of the Rule 98 bis procedure, which is directly related, in our view, to the presumption of innocence. If there is no case to answer at the end of the presentation of the case for the Prosecution, it would be contrary to the presumption of innocence and it would be unfair to require an accused to present a defence. That is why, Mr. President, the language in Rule 98 bis refers to the word "shall." For any count for which there is no evidence at the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall enter a judgement of acquittal. Consequently, Mr. President, although my submissions today deal only with counts 7, 8 and 2, we -- it is our understanding that it is the duty of the Trial Chamber, if it finds that there is no evidence to sustain the other counts, that the accused should also be acquitted of these further counts. I move directly to count number 7, forcible transfer. Quickly, the background to this count is as follows: In our response to the Prosecution motion to amend the indictments, that was on 21 July 2005, as well as in our motion alleging defects in the form of the consolidated amended indictment on 29 December 2005, we argued, Mr. President, that the alleged joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica enclave and to forcibly remove the population from the Zepa enclave were distinct from each other. We also argue that the Prosecution should not have been authorised to add a count of forcible transfer from the Zepa enclave to the charges laid against Drago Nikolic at that time. Our submission, Mr. President, rested on the fact that Drago Nikolic never set foot in Zepa and never had any involvement whatsoever in the events which led to the forcible transfer of the Zepa population. To be more precise, the alleged forcible transfer of the Zepa population. At that time, the Trial Chamber ruled that proof of the allegation of the existence of one joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclave, was a matter to be of evidence to be determined at trial. Well, here we are, Mr. President. We've heard the Prosecution evidence. And to us, the conclusion will remain the same. In the decision I was referring to, of course, was a Trial Chamber decision on the indictment of 31 May 2006, at paragraph 54. In that same decision, the Trial Chamber held at paragraph 52 that in the indictment, the Prosecution had pleaded with enough detail the time periods of the existence of the two alleged joint criminal enterprises, the two GCE being first the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and the second JCE, the joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men of Srebrenica. In our submission, Mr. President, it follows from the above that a distinction must be made between the two joint criminal enterprises alleged in the indictment, and I refer here to attachment A, paragraphs 96 and 97. Again, I repeat, the first one -- or the first joint criminal enterprise being the forcible transfer or deportation of the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa, and the second joint criminal enterprise being or referring to the killing of the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. The distinction between the two is highlighted in various paragraphs of the indictment, including, amongst others, paragraph 34, related to count 2, conspiracy to commit genocide. The second consideration arising from the indictment is that the joint criminal enterprise related to forcible transfer, as well as the Trial Chamber's decision and the indictment, all confirm that its aim was to remove the population from both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Both of these considerations, Mr. President, we submit are highly relevant for the Trial Chamber's adjudication of our submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis. I now move to the precise wording of count number 7 found in paragraph 49 of the indictment. Pursuant to this paragraph, Drago Nikolic is charged, together with others, for being a member of and knowingly participating in a joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was to force the Muslim population out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to areas outside the control of the RS from about 8 March 1995 through the end of August 1995. For the Trial Chamber to return a guilty finding against Drago Nikolic for count number 7, forcible transfer, it is our submission that the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt each of the following essential elements of the offence. If I may have 3D304 on e-court, please, page 1. It is our submission, Mr. President, that the following essential elements must be proved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. It's still not up yet. Yes, it is now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. From about 8 -- now, we have applied these essential elements to the facts of the case so that we can best present our submissions specifically as they apply to Drago Nikolic. From about 8 March through the end of August, 1995, the Bosnian Muslim population was unlawfully forced to leave the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Number 2, such forcible transfer was committed willfully, meaning with the intent to permanently remove the population, which implies the intention that they should not return once the situation has normalised or had normalised in the area. Regarding the permanent character of the removal of the population, we wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the commentary to the Geneva Conventions -- the commentary to Geneva Convention 4, to be more precise, at page 280, which states that unlike deportation and forcible transfer, evacuation is a provisional measure. So what must be proved is that the measure was permanent and that it was not evacuation. A distinction must be made between forcible transfer and evacuation. And as we will see later, this is another important consideration. The third element being the forcible transferred after -- during an armed conflict, and the forcible transfer occurred, according to the fourth element, in the context of a widespread, systematic attack against any civilian population. With respect to the fourth essential element, the Defence emphasizes the importance of the victim group being a civilian population. We refer the Trial Chamber to the judgement in the Sljivancanin -- the Prosecutor versus Sljivancanin in this regard. The fifth element, Mr. President, I'm sure we can see it -- yes we have it on the screen, there's a nexus between the forcible transfer and the attack on the civilian population. And finally, of course, the accused incurs individual criminal responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute, and that is for committing, planning, instigating, ordering, or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of the forcible transfer. Regarding this last element, Mr. President, the Defence recalls the Prosecution's theory in this case is that Drago Nikolic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise which, in the Prosecutor's view, is a way of committing forcible transfer. Mr. President, it is our submission that there is presently no evidence on the record that Drago Nikolic either participated or had any involvement in the alleged forcible transfer from both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It is also our submission that there is no evidence that Drago Nikolic had the required mens rea, in other words, the intent to permanently remove the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves. In fact, Mr. President, it is our submission that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude at this stage that Drago Nikolic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from both enclaves. Moreover, even though the indictment comprises no specific allegations to this effect, it is our submission that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic aided and abetted in any way the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from both enclaves. I will now explain why this is so, and I will begin by the alleged forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica. In order to understand the forcible transfer count, it is necessary, in our submission, to view the persons living in the Srebrenica enclave at the time as comprising three different groups; firstly, the women, children, and elderly who allegedly went from Srebrenica to Potocari before being transported by bus to Kladanj; secondly, the able-bodied men who were separated from the group that made its way from Srebrenica to Potocari before being allegedly transported to and detained in Bratunac; thirdly, the members of the Muslim 28th Division, the able-bodied men, and any other persons accompanying them who decided to leave the Srebrenica enclave with a view to reaching the territory under the control of the 2nd Corps of the Muslim Army in Tuzla. It is our submission, Mr. President, that count 7, forcible transfer, applies only to the first of these groups, namely, the women, children and elderly who allegedly went from Srebrenica to Potocari before being transported by bus to Kladanj. This submission, in our view, is confirmed by the fact that, on one hand, the able-bodied men allegedly separated in Potocari, and of course the soldiers and able-bodied men who intended to reach Muslim territory, are those targeted by the second joint criminal enterprise, which was allegedly to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica that were captured or surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July 1995. These able-bodied men, Mr. President, are, in our view, not included in the Bosnian Muslim population allegedly forcibly transferred from Srebrenica. This submission is also confirmed by the fact that the able-bodied men who were allegedly separated and detained in Bratunac, that this did not amount to forcible transfer, but that it was rather a detention issue, albeit possibly related to the joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. It is our submission that there was certainly no intention to transfer the able-bodied men separated in Potocari to an area outside the control of the Republika Srpska. As for the third group, the first consideration is that their departure from Srebrenica is not forcible transfer, as these persons did have a genuine choice to remain in Srebrenica. Most of them were armed, and they could remain in Srebrenica in order to fight. It was their decision to depart to reach the territory under the control of the 2nd Corps of the Muslim Army. Moreover, Mr. President, while this group was on its way to Tuzla, it represented a threat to the VRS and the Serb population in the area. This was confirmed by the evidence, and this is what led to the use of force by the VRS and the special police, first, to stop their progression towards Tuzla, and to detain them as prisoners of war. Once again, Mr. President, the capture and/or surrender of the members of the column did not amount to forcible transfer. This was rather legitimate military action possibly related, albeit, to the joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. And once again there was certainly no intention to transfer the able-bodied men from the column to an area outside the control of the Republika Srpska, which is alleged in this joint criminal enterprise. In any event, Mr. President, as will be seen later, even if it was considered that count 7, forcible transfer, does apply to the able-bodied men separated in Potocari and to the soldiers and able-bodied men who were in the column, it is our submission that the conclusion would be the same; that is, based on the evidence on the record at the close of the Prosecution case, there is no evidence which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that Drago Nikolic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, the purpose of which was to forcibly transfer these able-bodied men to an area outside the control of the Republika Srpska. I now move quickly to factual allegations in the indictment in relation to count 7, forcible transfer. These allegations are divided in two categories: Firstly, paragraphs 50 to 60, which concern the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population both from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves; secondly, paragraph 61 to 64, which deal specifically with the following: The alleged forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica; the alleged separation of the able-bodied men from the group which assembled in Potocari; and, three, the capture and/or surrender of the soldiers and able-bodied men from the column after the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July. Having reviewed the totality of the evidence on the record, including both the witness testimony and the documentary evidence, and focusing specifically on the intercept evidence as well as all of the logbooks admitted on the record, and I refer to the four logbooks, the operations duty officer logbook, the barracks duty officer logbook, the Zvornik Brigade forward command post duty officer logbook, as well as the Zvornik Brigade war diary, and having considered this evidence at its highest value in accordance with Rule 98 bis, it is our respectful submission, firstly, that there may be some evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica was transferred to Kladanj, an area outside the control of the Republika Srpska. But what is more important, Mr. President, there is no evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic either had any involvement in the events and/or activities described in these paragraphs or that he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, the aim of which was to transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica enclave. Regarding the first group, the group that we say was targeted by the first joint criminal enterprise, namely, the women, children, and elderly allegedly forcibly transferred to Kladanj, there was no involvement, Mr. President, of the Zvornik Brigade in this forcible transfer, leading to the conclusion that Drago Nikolic was also not involved. This was confirmed by the Prosecution military expert, Richard Butler, pages 20388-389. I would like to now address why this is so and what supports this conclusion. Firstly, regarding the 1st Battalion, which was assembled or put together from personnel taken from various units of the Zvornik Brigade, I refer to the group which participated in Operation Krivaja-95 under the command of Vinko Pandurevic, while this group may have been involved in the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population, this battalion was at the time under the command and control of the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic, and no longer under the command and control of the Zvornik Brigade, per se, as revealed by the evidence. In any event, there is no evidence on the record which could allow for the conclusion that Drago Nikolic was either a member of this battalion or involved in any way in the planning and/or preparations leading to the deployment of this battalion to take part in Operation Krivaja-95. Moreover, it stems from the evidence on the record and the testimony of Witness PW-168 that the Zvornik Brigade was not informed in any detail of the activities of this battalion while deployed on Operation Krivaja-95. Another issue which might be of interest to the Trial Chamber pertains to buses which would have been provided by the Zvornik Brigade. While there is some evidence on the record that the Drina Corps requested the Zvornik Brigade to provide buses and minibuses for its use on 12 July 1995, and that the Zvornik Brigade would have provided two buses and four trucks in response to this request, it is our submission that there is no evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the Zvornik Brigade was thus knowingly involved in the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica or in any other related criminal activity. This conclusion stems from the following: Firstly, Witness PW-168 testified that he knew that these vehicles were needed for the evacuation, and I stress the word "evacuation," of residents of Srebrenica pursuant to an agreement that had been reached, and that it was their wish to be transferred to Kladanj. Secondly, the request from the Drina Corps, I refer to Exhibit 110, referred to the evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, a legitimate purpose pursuant to the Geneva Conventions. Thirdly, the Drina Corps request was considered legitimate, from a military standpoint, by the Prosecution military expert, Richard Butler. Page 20389. Next, the drivers of these vehicles, once they left the Zvornik Brigade, they were under the command and control of the requesting party, namely, the Drina Corps commander, confirmed by Richard Butler, page 20398. Next, once the Zvornik Brigade was informed that Srebrenica had fallen, there is no evidence on the record that anyone from the Zvornik Brigade was aware that forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica was taking place. In any event, on that day, 12 July 1995, the evidence reveals that Drago Nikolic was not present. This was confirmed by Witness PW-168, by the -- by Witness Richard Butler, pages 20338-20339, as well as Exhibit 3DP311. The evidence also reveals that Drago Nikolic was not involved in sending vehicles to the Drina Corps; Butler, pages 20398-20399. Another issue which might be of interest to the Trial Chamber is that there is some evidence on the record that the Drina Corps requested the Zvornik Brigade to provide a squad of military policemen to perform traffic control duties at the Konjevic Polje intersection. I refer to Exhibit 157. Of course, in response to this request, there is some evidence that the Zvornik Brigade sent four or five military policemen, as many as could fit in one car according to Witness PW-168, to Konjevic Polje to perform traffic control duties. There is no evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the Zvornik Brigade was thus, by sending four or five military policemen for traffic control duties, knowingly involved in the forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica or in any other related criminal activity. This conclusion stems from the following: Witness PW-168 testified that he was in Memici when the order was received and the military policemen were sent. He did not speak to Drago Nikolic on this issue; page 17049. He does not know who sent the military policemen. The squad was either under the command and control of the Drina Corps or of the protection regiment; page 15823. And Witness PW-168 knows that Drago Nikolic had a day off on 12 July. Richard Butler testified that the order to send military policemen was, in his word, standard military order and that there was nothing improper about it; page 20392, and that Drago Nikolic was not involved in sending those military policemen; pages 19807, 19809. In any event, on that day, again the 12 July 1995, the evidence reveals that Drago Nikolic was not present. Again, this was confirmed by Witness PW-168, by Richard Butler, and by Exhibit 3DP311. Mr. President, it follows from the above that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude, and I refer specifically here to the first group, the women, children and the elderly, that anyone in the Zvornik Brigade, including Drago Nikolic, was knowingly involved in the forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica. Furthermore, there is no evidence on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic had any involvement whatsoever in the forcible transfer of the Muslim population, group 1, from the Srebrenica enclave. So what is the situation concerning the other two groups, the able-bodied men separated in Potocari and the soldiers and able-bodied men from the column? Should the Trial Chamber conclude that count 7, forcible transfer, also applies to them. As mentioned earlier, it is our submission that the conclusion remains the same; that is, there is still no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica enclave to an area outside the control of RS. This conclusion stems now from the following: First, there was no involvement of the Zvornik Brigade. The 1st Battalion deployed on the Operation Krivaja-95, referred to earlier, was neither involved in fighting the column, nor in the capture or surrender of the members thereof. In fact, there is no -- based on the evidence on the record, no element of the Zvornik Brigade was involved in the capture, surrender and detention, that is, both in Bratunac and other sites along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road of the able-bodied men from the column. Moreover, looking at the information available to the Zvornik Brigade concerning the capture, surrender and detention of soldiers and able-bodied men from the column, there is some information in this regard in the duty officer's -- in the duty operation officer's logbook. There is, nonetheless, no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the Zvornik Brigade had any knowledge that anything other than proper military activity was being conducted with respect to the column. Moreover, there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic had any knowledge or was involved in any way in the capture, surrender, and detention of able-bodied men from the column.
