I now move, Mr. President, to forcible transfer from the Zepa enclave. I begin with the factual allegations in the indictment, which are found at paragraphs 65 to 71. These paragraphs deal specifically with the alleged forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Zepa. Once again, Mr. President, having reviewed the totality of the evidence on the record, as mentioned earlier, focusing on the intercepts and the logbooks, witness evidence and documents, and having considered this evidence at its highest value, it is our respectful submission that there may be some evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt at this stage that the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa was forcibly transferred to an area outside the control of RS, but what is more important, once again, there is no evidence on the record which could allow a reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic either had any involvement in the events and/or activities described in these paragraphs, or that he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, the aim of which was to transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Zepa enclave. In our submission, this conclusion stems from the following: While there may be some evidence that the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, or, sorry, the 1st Battalion assembled from members taken from units of the Zvornik Brigade may have been involved in preparations leading to attacks on the Zepa enclaves. The evidence reveals that this battalion was withdrawn from the area of Zepa and returned to the area of Zvornik before any force or threat of the use of force was applied on Zepa with the aim of forcibly transferring the Muslim population from that enclave. Moreover, as mentioned earlier, Drago Nikolic was not a member of this battalion and he was not involved in the planning or preparations leading to the deployment of this battalion. In any event, until this battalion was returned from Zepa, this -- it was under the command and control of the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic. Furthermore, there is no evidence on the record that Drago Nikolic was ever involved in the events which took place in Zepa or ever informed of the events which took place in Zepa. This was our conclusion before the beginning of this case, and there is no evidence on the record, now that the Prosecution has closed its case, which would allow for a different conclusion. It follows from the above, Mr. President, that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that anyone in the Zvornik Brigade, including Drago Nikolic, was knowingly involved in the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa, and there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic had any involvement whatsoever in the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from the Zepa enclave. While in our view, Mr. President, this demonstration is sufficient to justify a verdict of acquittal at this stage for count 7, forcible transfer, there is yet one more area we need to look at, namely, paragraph 80 of the indictment, which comprises the alleged role and actions of Drago Nikolic in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Srebrenica and Zepa Muslim population. Firstly, pursuant to paragraphs 80(a)(i) and (ii), it is alleged that Drago Nikolic was in control of the movement of the Muslim population out of the enclaves from 13 and 16 July by first assisting in the planning, organising, and supervising of the transportation of Muslim men from Bratunac and, two, supervising, facilitating, and overseeing the transportation of Muslim men once again from Bratunac to detention sites in the Zvornik area, always for the period from 13 to 16 July. Now that the Prosecution has closed its case, it is our respectful submission that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic was involved in controlling the transportation of Muslim men from Bratunac at any time. Moreover, should the Trial Chamber conclude that Drago Nikolic was in some way involved or that there is some evidence that could lead to this conclusion that Drago Nikolic may have been involved in the transport of prisoners during the period from 13 [Realtime transcript read in error "15"] To 16 July 1995, it is our submission that any such involvement of Drago Nikolic is related to the alleged joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica, those that were captured or who surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July 1995. Any such involvement is not related in any way to the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa. Secondly, pursuant to paragraph 80 and paragraph 80(a)(iii), it is also alleged that in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Srebrenica and Zepa Muslim population, firstly, that Drago Nikolic committed the acts comprised in paragraphs 30.6 to 30.12, 30.14, 30.15, 31.4, 32, and 34 to 37. It is also alleged that Drago Nikolic failed to ensure the safety and welfare of prisoners, which would have been his duty. Now, we don't know what area is covered by this paragraph, although it appears that it would be in the area of Zvornik. Should the Trial Chamber conclude at this stage that there is some evidence leading to the conclusion that Drago Nikolic may have been involved in any of these acts or omissions, it is our submission that any such involvement of Drago Nikolic is once again related to the joint -- to the alleged, sorry, joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica, those who were captured or who surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July 1995, and accordingly that any such involvement of Drago Nikolic is not related in any way to the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Srebrenica and Zepa Muslim population. These acts, Mr. President, were either committed after 13 July, at a time when the forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica would have been completed, and before the alleged forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Zepa would have taken place. As mentioned at the beginning, the Prosecution's theory in this case is based on the existence of two joint criminal enterprise, and it is crucial not to mix the two in all fairness to the accused. In this regard, it is our submission that the analysis to be performed by the Trial Chamber in order to adjudicate on our application pursuant to Rule 98 bis, is to assess whether there is any evidence on the record on the basis of which it could conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Pursuant to the case law of the International Tribunal, membership in a joint criminal enterprise depends on the following requirements. If I can have in e-court, please, 3D304, page 3. Mr. President, I take this opportunity to highlight an error in the transcript. At page 53, line 16, there's is a mistake. It is my understanding, from what I'm given, is that it says lines 13 to 16, and -- it's not 15, it's 13 to 16. The following requirements must be met for somebody to be found to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise: First, a plurality of persons participated in the forcible transfer of the population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves; second, the existence of a common plan, design, or purpose to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves; three, that the accused participated in the common plan, design, or purpose, the aim of which was to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and, four, the accused shared the purpose of the alleged joint criminal enterprise; that is, the accused intended to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Applying these elements to the evidence on the record at this stage, it is our submission that there is no direct evidence on the record that Drago Nikolic shared the purpose of the forcible transfer, joint criminal enterprise, and that he intended to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to an area outside the control of the Republika Srpska. Moreover, even if the Trial Chamber was to conclude that at this stage there is some evidence which could allow the Trial Chamber to conclude that Drago Nikolic may have been a member of the joint criminal enterprise to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica, those that were captured or who surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica, a conclusion of course we contest and we are confident will not be shown beyond a reasonable doubt at the end of the trial, it would not allow for the conclusion or the inference, whether direct or from circumstantial evidence, that Drago Nikolic intended to forcibly transfer the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Moreover, looking at the participation component of "joint criminal enterprise," that is, joint criminal enterprise category 1, one of the following must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt to support a finding that the accused participated in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Either the accused personally committed the forcible transfer as a principal offender. There is absolutely no evidence of this on the record. Either the accused assisted or encouraged the principal offender in committing the forcible transfer. There is no evidence of this, either. Or, three, the accused acted in furtherance of the common plan to forcibly transfer by reason of his position of authority or function, with knowledge of the nature of that system of forcible transfer and the intent to further it. It is our submission that there is no evidence on the record at this stage on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic met any of these three forms of participation in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Consequently, Mr. President, if the participation of Drago Nikolic in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves is not a possible conclusion at this stage, the final question then is: Could a reasonable trier of fact conclude, on the basis of the evidence on the record, that Drago Nikolic aided and abetted the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves? It is our submission that the answer to this question is, "No." If I can have 3D304, page 4, on e-court, please. These elements of aiding and abetting are well established in the case law of the Tribunal. I only put it up on e-court to highlight that any acts committed by an accused would have to amount to practical assistance which had a substantial effect on the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population. Pursuant to the evidence on the record, it is our submission that there is no evidence of any acts committed by Drago Nikolic which had a substantial effect on the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It is significant, in this respect, that neither Dragan Obrenovic, the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade, nor Dragan Djukic, the chief of the Zvornik Brigade, were indicted for the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. While the Prosecution's decision to indict or not these individuals for the forcible transfer of the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa, is of course discretionary in nature, the fact that they were not charged for forcible transfer is nonetheless a powerful indicator that Drago Nikolic was not involved in any way in these activities. One last consideration, Mr. President. At the time the idea of forcible transfer first came up, that is, in Potocari earlier in July, Drago Nikolic was not even -- sorry, the evidence on the record is silent regarding either the presence or the activities of Drago Nikolic at that time. This alleged plan or common purpose, if it was elaborated at such a time, Drago Nikolic was not at that time involved in any event. It is simply, Mr. President, a further consideration. I now move, Mr. President, to count number 8, deportation of the Muslim population from Zepa. I will go quickly, in light of the arguments and submissions presented with respect to count 7, forcible transfer, it is our respectful submission that there is presently no evidence on the record that Drago Nikolic either participated or had any involvement in the alleged deportation from Zepa, and there is no evidence that Drago Nikolic had the required mens rea, in other words, the intent to deport the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa. In fact, it is our submission that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude at this stage that Drago Nikolic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise to deport the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa. Furthermore, it is our submission, even though the indictment comprises no specific allegations to this effect, that there is no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic aided and abetted in any way the deportation of the Bosnian Muslim population from Zepa. Mr. President, regarding deportation, it is my understanding that counsel representing other accused in this case will be presenting legal arguments, showing that a deportation count simply cannot hold. And without going into these arguments, we simply say that we join the arguments which will be presented by counsel representing other accused in this regard. In conclusion, Mr. President, regarding counts 7, forcible transfer from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to areas outside the control of the RS, and count 8, deportation of the Muslim population from the Zepa enclave, we submit, Mr. President, that there is no case to answer for Drago Nikolic and that he must be acquitted at this stage of both of these counts in full. I now move quickly to count number 2, conspiracy to commit genocide, alleged in paragraphs 34 and 35 of the indictment. Pursuant to paragraph 34, Drago Nikolic would be responsible for having entered into an agreement with several others, firstly, to kill the able-bodied men from Srebrenica that were captured or surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July 1995, and, secondly, to remove the remaining Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa from the Republika Srpska, thirdly, with the intent to destroy those Muslims. The background to this charge, Mr. President, is as follows: In the Prosecution's motion for amendments to the indictments, dated 28 June 2005, the Prosecution requested to remove the charge of complicity in genocide and to add a new count of conspiracy to commit genocide. The Prosecution justified the new count of conspiracy to commit genocide on the basis of developments in the law regarding conspiracy and the fact that the law on joint criminal enterprise at the time, in any event, was in a state of flux. The conspiracy to commit genocide charge is a first before the International Tribunal. Moreover, even though the Prosecution cites a number of cases in its pre-trial brief where conspiracy to commit genocide charges were laid before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, in most of these cases, and I refer here to footnote 585 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, the charge of conspiracy to commit genocide has been removed from the indictment and thus is not discussed at all in those decisions. Strikingly, in its discussion on the count of conspiracy to commit genocide, the Prosecution omitted in this footnote and in his arguments the following two cases in which the accused was acquitted of conspiracy to commit genocide at the Rule 98 bis stage, even though they were later convicted of genocide. Case ICTR 99-54, Alpha-Trial, Jean de Dieu, Kamuhanda; the second case, ICTR 99-46-Trial, Samuel -- and I apologise for my pronunciation, Imanishimwe. It is our submission that these cases are especially relevant to this case and the situation of Drago Nikolic. We also refer the Trial Chamber to the following three cases in which the accused were acquitted of conspiracy to commit genocide, this time in the final judgements. The Prosecutor versus Alfred Musema, the Prosecutor versus Elizaphan and Gerard Nrakirutimana, and the Prosecutor versus Juvenal Kajelijeli. For the Trial Chamber to return a guilty finding against Drago Nikolic for count number 2, conspiracy to commit genocide, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt each of the following essential elements of the offence. If I can have 3D304, page 5, in e-court, please. The first element: The accused entered into an agreement with others to kill the able-bodied Muslim men of Srebrenica that were captured or surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on the 11 July 1995 and removed the remaining population of Srebrenica and Zepa from the Republika Srpska. The second element: The accused had the required mental element for genocide. As a preliminary consideration, Mr. President, I wish to state for the record that our submissions in relation to count 2 at this stage are not related in any way to the genocide count, nor to the essential elements of genocide which must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt for an accused to be convicted of that charge. At this stage, our application, pursuant to Rule 98 bis, does not address genocide. It only addresses conspiracy to commit genocide, and taking into consideration the essential element of this count, conspiracy to commit genocide, and as mentioned earlier, having reviewed the totality of the evidence on the record, including the witness testimony and the documentary evidence, and considered this evidence at its highest value, it is our respectful submission that there is absolutely no evidence on the record on the basis of which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Drago Nikolic entered into an agreement with others to commit genocide. Our submission rests on the following: There is some evidence on the records concerning wrongdoings or alleged wrongdoings of Drago Nikolic. We simply say that we take all of the evidence and we take it at its highest value. We simply cannot conclude that Drago Nikolic entered into an agreement to commit genocide with others. If we look at the two cases before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in which the accused were acquitted of conspiracy to commit genocide at the Rule 98 bis stage, and we invite the Trial Chamber to look at the specific involvement of these two accused, the conclusions of the Trial Chamber regarding their involvement, when they were found guilty of genocide later on, this was evidence on the record at the Rule 98 bis stage, yet those Trial Chambers could not conclude, on the basis of evidence related to such involvement of these two accused, that they had entered into an agreement to commit genocide. Consequently, our submission is that -- or our submissions are geared towards the actus reus of conspiracy to commit genocide, the agreement part. If we compare any evidence on the record concerning alleged wrongdoings of Drago Nikolic with the type of involvement upon which Trial Chambers in ICTR could not find that there was an agreement or that those accused had entered into an agreement, our submission is simply as follows: It simply cannot be concluded, based on any of these alleged wrongdoings of Drago Nikolic, that he did enter into an agreement to commit genocide, and we focus here on the actus reus of the conspiracy to commit genocide. In conclusion, Mr. President, it is our submission that there is no case to answer concerning conspiracy to commit genocide regarding specifically Drago Nikolic. There's lots of evidence that can be taken into consideration to justify this conclusion, such as the level of the accused as a junior officer and second lieutenant, such as the knowledge of the accused of either directive 7 or directive 7-1, so not only what he may allegedly have done wrong, but also the over all context of this case, and it is our submission that you simply cannot conclude that he entered into that agreement, and that he must be acquitted of this count at this stage. In conclusion, Mr. President, we invite you to return, at the end of these Rule 98 bis proceedings, a verdict of acquittal for counts 2, 7, and 8, and order that the trial can continue on the basis of counts 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6. And I take this opportunity to mention that we are confident that at the end of this trial, it will not be possible for the Trial Chamber to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt on the guilt of the accused for any of these other counts. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the oral arguments under Rule 98 bis, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence will abide by the standards established in the jurisprudence of the present Tribunal, avoiding the repetition of the arguments presented by my learned colleague Mr. Bourgon related to the 98 bis jurisprudence. In light of the limited scope of the analysis under this Rule and the fact that it is impossible to present detailed allegations for all the counts of the indictment in the time that we have for our presentation, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence will limit itself only to counts 2 and 8 of the indictment. Mr. Borovcanin's Defence would like to stress that there is no direct evidence proving that Mr. Borovcanin, first, entered into any kind of agreement with any person about the commission of crimes; second, ordered anyone to commit any crime; and, third, personally committed any crime or instigated or in any other way aided and abetted the planning, preparation and commission of the crimes he has been charged with under the indictment. Conspiracy to commit genocide is an agreement on the part of two or more persons with the aim of committing the crime of genocide. This definition is quoted from the Niyitegeka and others case, the appeals judgement, case number ICTR-99-46A. The date is the 7th of July, 2006, paragraph 92. The actus reus of this crime is the entering into the agreement itself. As for the mens rea of this crime, it is the intention to enter into such agreement. This is a quote from the Nahimana et al case, the appeal judgement. The case number is ICTR-99-52- A, the date is 28th of November, 2007, paragraph 894. And another case, the Bagosora et al case, the number is ICTR-98-41-T. It is the decision on Rule 98 bis. The date is the 2nd of February, 2005. Paragraph 12. In count 2 of the indictment, laid out in greater detail in paragraphs 34 through 37, Ljubomir Borovcanin is charged with the crime conspiracy to commit genocide, punishable under Article 4(3)(b) of the Statute. In paragraph 34 of the indictment, it is alleged that Mr. Borovcanin entered an agreement with several other persons, including Radovan Karadzic, Milenko Zivanovic, Radislav Krstic, Zdravko Tolimir, and the other accused in the present case, whose names are listed in Annex A to the indictment, to kill able-bodied Muslim men from Srebrenica who had been captured or had surrendered after the fall of Srebrenica on the 11th of July, 1995, and to remove the remaining Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa from Republika Srpska in order to destroy those Muslims. Further, in the same paragraph, it is alleged that the facts -- the underlying facts for this count of the indictment are the same as the facts alleged in the indictment in relation to the joint criminal enterprise. And in the next paragraph, paragraph 35, it is further alleged that the agreement was entered with the intent to destroy, in part, the Bosnian Muslims as a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, as such. In paragraph 36 of the indictment, it is alleged that Ljubomir Borovcanin, together with the other officers in units of the VRS and the MUP, listed in annex A of the indictment, actually implemented the conspiracy and the joint criminal enterprise, and that he was a conscious participant in the enterprise which was aimed at the summary execution and burial of thousands of captured Bosnian Muslim men and boys. It is alleged further that the initial plan was to execute summarily more than 1.000 Muslim men aged between 16 and 60 who were separated from the rest of the population on the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995. But on the 12th or the 13th of July, the plan encompassed the summary execution of more than 6.000 Muslim men and boys taken prisoner from the column in which they tried to flee the Srebrenica enclave in the period between the 12th of July and the 1st of November, 1995, or about that date. Further, in paragraph 37, it is alleged that Mr. Borovcanin and the other participants in the enterprise could have envisaged that in the course of and after the joint criminal enterprise, the VRS and MUP forces would commit isolated, opportunistic murders and persecutions described in paragraphs 31 through 48 of the indictment. The indictment further alleges that the alleged plan to murder hundreds of Muslims in Potocari had been elaborated by Mladic and others in the evening hours of the 11th of July and in the morning of the 12th of July, 1995, and this plan was allegedly extended or amended to include a large number of Muslim men who had started surrendering to the Serb forces in other locations on the 12th of July. I'm quoting from paragraphs 27 and 29 of the indictment. The Defence would like to note that there is no specific information in the indictment as to where and, in particular, with which other persons this agreement was entered into, and whether this was an explicit or an implicit, tacit agreement. In the pre-trial brief submitted by the Prosecution, we find no additional details regarding this issue. The Defence would like to state that in the course of its case, the Prosecution failed to adduce any evidence that would show where or indeed when Mr. Borovcanin allegedly entered into this agreement. Even if the Prosecution believes that it did call some circumstantial evidence, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence would like to show this Trial Chamber the ruling standard and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal regarding reliance on circumstantial evidence; to wit, in the appeal judgement in the Nahimana et al case, the so-called "media case," the number is ICTR-99-52-A, the date is the 28th of November, 2007, this is how the Appeals Chamber commented on the use of indirect or circumstantial evidence used to prove conspiracy to commit genocide: "The question at this stage for the Appeals Chamber is to know whether, insofar as such institutional coordination has been established, a reasonable trier of fact could conclude thereof that the only reasonable inference would be to say that this institution coordination was a result of a resolution to act with a view to commit genocide, but there is no doubt that all these factual findings are compatible with the existence of a common goal, aiming at committing genocide. Nonetheless, we are not only providing here the only reasonable inference." Paragraph 910. This test, applied by the Appeals Chamber, is similar to the standard that should be applied at this stage in the proceedings, in accordance to Rule 98 bis, which reads: "Would any reasonable trier of fact be able to convict on the basis of the evidence presented?" Revising the conclusion of the Trial Chamber regarding the conspiracy, the Appeals Chamber in the Nahimana et al case stressed the following: "The Appeals Chamber holds that even if these elements can coincide with a degree of agreement between the participants with a view to committing genocide, nevertheless it is not enough to just establish that such an agreement has been made beyond any reasonable doubt." Paragraph 906. The conspiracy requires the existence of an actual real agreement entered into by several persons. Although this agreement may be implicit or tacit, it has to be a real agreement, and its objective must be the commission of a crime. The importance of this criterion stems from the fact that the crime was committed by the very dint of entering into an agreement. Unlike the joint criminal enterprise in this case, the perpetrators need not actually succeed in committing the crime, the underlying crime, in order to -- for their guilt to be established, their guilt for conspiracy. And here I quote the Nahimana et al case, Appeal Judgement 894, that's the judgement from 2007, Bagosora et al, ICTR-98-41-T, the 98 bis decision, the decision dated the 2nd of February, 2005, paragraph 12; Bizimungu et al, the case number is ICTR-99-50-T, a 98 bis decision dated the 22nd of November, 2005, paragraph 23; the Niyitegeka case, the number is ICTR-96-14, the date is the 16th of May, 2003, the paragraph is 423. In summary, the agreement itself constitutes a crime. Mr. Borovcanin's Defence claims that no reasonable trier of fact would be able to conclude, on the basis of circumstantial evidence presented in court, that Mr. Borovcanin entered into any kind of agreement to commit genocide with anyone. This allegation, I'm talking about the allegation that he actually entered into an agreement, is indeed quite incredible for the following reasons: If this alleged plan to kill able-bodied Muslims from Srebrenica is a result of an agreement, in the opinion of the Prosecution, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence would like to stress that in the course of the Prosecution case, no evidence was called to corroborate in any way the claim that Mr. Borovcanin had actually entered into such an agreement in any way. To support this argument, the Defence would like to invoke the fact that in the course of its case, the Prosecution failed to prove that Mr. Borovcanin had been present at any meeting where such an agreement might have been reached. It likewise failed to call any evidence to prove that if any such agreement existed, that Mr. Borovcanin was in fact aware of it. As for this fact, the Defence relies on the evidence of Witness -- Prosecution Witness Zoran Petrovic, a journalist with Studio B Independent Television, who during the course of his stay in the Srebrenica and Bratunac area on the 13th of July 1995 accompanied Mr. Borovcanin at almost all times. So if the position taken by the Prosecutor and expressed in the indictment is correct, that is, that in the night between the 11th and the 12th July 1995, Mr. Borovcanin entered into an agreement with other participants to commit genocide, which alleged agreement was extended at a later stage on the 13th of July, a logical question is: Why would Mr. Borovcanin, if he had known of such an agreement and accepted it, have allowed a journalist from an independent TV channel to come to this area and to film everything that he considered to be of interest? The fact -- the very fact that this reporter, Mr. Petrovic, was present in this area where, on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, the fighting was still going on, and the footage that he made on that occasion and that this Trial Chamber has had an occasion to see in the course of the Prosecution case several times, and the fact that the footage taken by Mr. Petrovic was broadcast on Studio B, a Belgrade TV channel, confirm that Mr. Borovcanin did not know and could not have known what would actually be happening in this period. All of this confirms that Mr. Borovcanin did not enter into any kind of agreement for the commission of the crime of genocide, as alleged in the indictment. In this respect, the Defence would like to quote short excerpts from the transcript of Mr. Petrovic's testimony which best serve to illustrate the claim that Mr. Borovcanin did not know at all what would be happening in those days. In the examination-in-chief, answering the Prosecution questions, Witness Petrovic stated, at transcript page 18811, on the 5th of December, 2007, the following: [In English] "As far as I know, he was physically and mentally in good health. Otherwise, only a madman would work against himself to his own detriment to film something if you know that your own lot are planning to kill somebody or do something improper. This is something I think is only proper of me to tell you. I think it's a rare thing that somebody would allow you to do something like that, even in the US Army." [Interpretation] Furthermore, in the examination-in-chief on the 5th of December, 2007, the same witness, at transcript page 18804, stated the following, and I quote: [In English] "Now, did Mr. Borovcanin ever try to censor what you were filming, or, tell you to 'film this, don't film that,' or were you completely freelance independent in what you took video of?" Answer: "Now we are coming to what I wanted to ask you. Do you think that anyone -- anyone who is in their right mind would allow a journalist to film war crimes and to leave him alive? Do you think it's -- it would be a normal thing for me to sit here, as I do sit today, had this indeed happened? Did you ever see, and let's refer to this most recent war in Iraq, did you ever see anyone film anything from 2003 onwards, anything of the sort? Did you ever see a journalist, especially an embedded one, film anything of the sort? So why should this army react differently? All the rules of the military are the same. He permitted me to work, and I didn't have any reason to tell the untruth, and that was reason enough for this individual to let me film this. Perhaps some others wouldn't have allowed me to. It was down to mutual respect." [Interpretation] And, finally, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence would like to quote another segment of the evidence provided by this witness in the cross-examination on the 6th of December, 2007. The page reference is 18858 and 18859: [In English] "I was just interested in your assessment and impression, so that will suffice as far as I'm concerned for the moment. And now just one more question with regards to the meadow in Sandici. You were free to film. Mr. Borovcanin never told you not to film the people in the meadow. He didn't say, 'Don't film what's going on there, don't film the people in the meadow,' nothing like that. Can you confirm that that was so?" Answer: "Of course he did not. Well, let me remind you, as I told Mr. Nicholls earlier on, I had two experiences with that unit during the war, and I conducted myself professionally. I did my job professionally, so there was no need for anybody to supervise me in any way, absolutely no need for them to supervise and see what I was filming if they had already given me permission to film." [Interpretation] So bearing in mind the standards that we've already presented, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence claims that the possibility or the probability that Mr. Borovcanin actually enter into an agreement to commit the crime of genocide is much less probable than the possibility that Mr. Borovcanin had no knowledge of the existence of any kind of agreement for the commission of this crime. And Mr. Borovcanin's Defence, therefore, proposes to this Trial Chamber to acquit Mr. Borovcanin on count 2 of the indictment, pursuant to Rule 98 bis. I am about to move on to our part of the presentation which has to do with count 8 of the indictment. Count 8 of the indictment charges Mr. Borovcanin with the crime of deportation as a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(d) of the Statute. Similar to forcible transfer, deportation is a forced displacement of civilians from an area in which they lawfully reside, in which case there is no basis allowed or envisaged within the framework of international law. Under the basis allowed by international law, we understand the basis provided in the Geneva Convention number 4 and protocol 2, the crime of deportation is different from forcible transfer, since in the case of deportation, it is necessary that the population is being displaced outside the territory it resides in, whilst with the transfer, this element does not exist. In all other elements, both crimes are identical. The crime of deportation, as envisaged by Article 5(d) of the ICTY's Statute, and according to the appeal judgement in the Stakic case, number IT-97-24-A of the 22nd March 2006, in paragraph 278 it states: "The actus reus of deportation is forcibly displacing persons by expelling them or using other types of force out of an area in which they lawfully reside across the djura, state boundary, or in certain situations across the de facto border, without the existence of the basis allowed by international legal regulation. The Appeal Chamber believes that it is not necessary that in order to have the required mens rea, the perpetrator intends to permanently displace these persons across the boundary. Forcible transfer, which can be seen as an underlying act in relation to other inhumane acts, pursuant to Article 5(i) of the Statute, is defined as a forcible displacement of persons which can take place within state boundaries, and I refer to the Stakic case appeal judgement and Naletilic appeal judgement, which is case IT-98-34-A of the 3rd of May, 2006, paragraph 154. Going by the title just above paragraph 50 of the indictment and all the way down to paragraph 71, one concludes that the Prosecution believe that the enterprise of forcibly removing the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa is a unified criminal enterprise. No evidence was adduced to that effect during their case. It is quite the contrary. It is the position of this Defence that during the Prosecution case, it was clearly established that the decision to execute a military attack against the Zepa enclave was made only after VRS forces had taken over the enclave of Srebrenica, and that up until that point, the only aim of the military operation of the VRS was to physically separate the two enclaves and to prevent communication between them, which was fully justified in military terms. Paragraph 84 of the indictment contains a Prosecution position on the fact that Mr. Borovcanin, together with the accused Popovic, Beara, Nikolic, Miletic, Gvero, and Pandurevic, allegedly committed the crime of deportation in the following way and by using the following means: By forcibly moving men, Bosnian Muslims, out of Zepa, across the Drina, into Serbia, due to unbearable conditions being imposed upon the enclave through limiting the supply of aid to the enclave and intimidating and terrorizing the population by shelling civilian areas and carrying out attacks on the enclave, as described in paragraph 71 of the indictment. Mr. Borovcanin's Defence will analyse this Prosecution hypothesis contained in paragraph 84(a) of the indictment and will analyse each of the alleged ways and means used to commit the crime of deportation, with a special focus on Mr. Borovcanin and the units he commanded. The first way which was used to allegedly commit the crime of deportation as a crime against humanity, the indictment states the creation of unbearable living conditions in the enclave of Zepa by limiting the supply of aid into the enclave. Not a single piece of evidence adduced during the Prosecution case points to the fact that either Mr. Borovcanin or any of his subordinate units had any direct or indirect influence on the distribution of aid to the enclave, and therefore they had no ability to limit it. When talking about forwarding aid to the Zepa enclave, it can only be viewed during the time period prior to the military operation, during which time neither Mr. Borovcanin nor any of his subordinate units were in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa. Something that was not in dispute from the outset of this proceedings between the Prosecution and Mr. Borovcanin's Defence is the fact that on the 11th of July, 1995, he arrived in the territory of Bratunac Municipality and that only after his arrival the units he commanded began arriving in the territory. Therefore, it is clear that Mr. Borovcanin had no ways to influence any alleged forwarding of the aid to the enclave. As another way or as the second way of committing the crime of deportation of the Bosnian Muslims from Zepa is the intimidation and terrorizing of the population by shelling civilian areas and carrying out attacks on the enclave, as described in paragraph 71 of the indictment. During the Prosecution case, not a shred of evidence was adduced that would point to the fact that either Mr. Borovcanin or any of his subordinate units participated in the shelling of any part of the enclave of Zepa, including, of course, the civilian areas of it, or that they participated in any attacks on the enclave. Concerning the aforementioned allegations of the indictment, namely, that the forcible removal of the Muslim population from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa presents a joint criminal enterprise, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence wishes to point to Exhibit P00181, which is an order of the Main Staff of the VRS of the 10th of July, 1995, sent to the Command of the Drina Corps and the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. In item 4 of the order, it is stated that offensive combat operations against the enclave of Zepa should begin on the 12th of July, 1995. It is obvious that the decision on such offensive operations, which could potentially lead to the military occupation of the Zepa enclave, was made only after the VRS forces managed to take over the enclave of Srebrenica, and until that time or, rather, before that, there could have been no plan in existence to occupy the Zepa enclave. From the same document, we can also see that none of the units commanded by Mr. Borovcanin was included in this order. This order was not sent to Mr. Borovcanin, even by way of information. In particular, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence wishes to point out that during the Prosecution case, there was no dispute between the Defence and Prosecution concerning some of the units commanded by Mr. Borovcanin participating in the combat at Baljkovica, which is in a different direction to the enclave of Zepa, and it is some 100 kilometres away from it. Therefore, during the Prosecution case, not a single piece of evidence was adduced which could point to the fact that Mr. Borovcanin in any way participated in any potential planning of attacks on the enclave of Zepa. Also, no evidence was adduced which would point to the fact that Mr. Borovcanin was informed of it or consulted by anyone within the VRS. Finally, this Defence would like to invoke the Prosecution's military expert's testimony, Mr. Richard Butler, of the 25th of January, 2008, page 20500. I quote: [In English] "When you were analysing the documents and as you were preparing your expert reports about the Zepa operation, you did not come by any proof about the participation of any units under the command of Mr. Borovcanin or his participation in the Zepa operation; is that true?" Answer: "Yes, sir, I have no information pertaining to Mr. Borovcanin's role in what we would call the Zepa operation." [Interpretation] Therefore, this Defence asserts that as regards Mr. Borovcanin, the Prosecution did not present a single piece of evidence which would corroborate count 8 of the indictment, this being the crime of deportation as a crime against humanity. Therefore, the Defence respectfully requests that Mr. Borovcanin, in keeping with Rule 98 bis, be acquitted on this count of the indictment. Nearing the end of our presentation, we would briefly like to refer to paragraph 31.1 of the indictment. The reason for it is the Prosecution motion which has to do with paragraph 31.1(b) of the indictment, submitted on the 25th October 2006; namely, in paragraph 31.1 of the indictment, under (a) and (b), we see the murder of nine Bosnian Muslims. Under (a), it is stated that their bodies were found in the woods near the UN compound on the Budak side of the main road, whereas under (b) it is stated that the bodies were found in a creek near the white house, some 700 metres from the UN compound. As I just said, the Prosecution, in its Prosecution motion regarding paragraph 31.1(b) of the indictment of the 25th of October, 2006, state that it is their position that this is one and the same event and that they will agree to a motion to issue a judgement of acquittal concerning subparagraph 31.1(b), which can be seen on page 2 of the motion. In addition to that, in paragraph 31.1(c), it is stated that in the morning of the 13th of July, the bodies of six Bosnian Muslim women and five Bosnian Muslim men were found in a stream near the UN compound in Potocari. Concerning this allegation of the indictment, not a single piece of evidence was adduced or tendered during their case. Therefore, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence respectfully suggest that the Chamber, in relation to paragraphs 31.1(b) and (c) issues a judgement of acquittal under Rule 98 bis. Your Honours, although Mr. Borovcanin's Defence decided to present its position only in relation to the aforementioned counts of the indictment, it in no way means that this Defence believes that the Prosecution proffered sufficient evidence based on which a reasonable trier of fact could ascertain the guilt of Mr. Borovcanin for any of the crimes he was charged with. Therefore, this Defence appeals to the Chamber to use its discretion and authority in making their decision whether a judgement of acquittal can be issued in relation to 98 bis as well as in relation to other counts of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.text: So we might finish tomorrow, basically, if you put Ms. Fauveau and Mr. Josse together, that may take a maximum of three hours, which would still leaves us the 35 minutes -- 45 minutes, sorry, for Mr. Haynes to finish his, which means that you're being put on notice that on Monday, you will be starting with your response.

We're not going to take the whole -- the whole time, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Bourgon, I thought you were --

utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd just like to at this time take this opportunity to seek leave from the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule 126, to reply to the response which was filed by the Prosecution to the joint Defence motion challenging the admissibility of the report of Richard Butler.
